edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De resurrectione carnis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.locus: On the Resurrection of the Flesh II
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Si vero et apud Deum aliqua secta est, Epicureis magis affinis quam prophetis, sciemus quid audiant a Christo Sadducaei. Christo enim servabatur, omnia retro occulta nudare, dubitata dirigere, praelibata supplere, praedicata repraesentare; mortuorum certe resurrectionem, non modo per semetipsum, verum etiam in semetipso probare. Nunc autem ad alios sadducaeos praeparamur, partiarios sententiae illorum. Ita dimidiam agnoscunt resurrectionem, solius scilicet animae; aspernati carnem, sicut et ipsum Dominum carnis. Nulli denique alii salutem corporali substantiae invident, quam alterius divinitatis haeretici. Ideoque et Christum aliter disponere coacti, ne creator carnis habeatur, in ipsa prius carne ejus erraverunt; aut nullius veritatis contendentes eam, secundum Marcionem et Basilidem; aut propriae qualitatis, secundum haereses Valentini, et Apellem. Atque ita sequitur, ut salutem ejus substantiae excludant, cujus Christum consortem negant; certi illam summo praejudicio resurrectionis instructam, si jam in Christo resurrexit caro. Propterea et nos volumen praemisimus De Carne Christi, quo eam et solidam probamus, adversum phantasmatis vanitatem, et humanam vindicamus, adversus qualitatis proprietatem; cujus conditio Christum et hominem, et filium hominis inscripserit. Carneum enim atque corporeum probantes eum, proinde et obducimus praescribendo nullum alium credendum Deum praeter Creatorem, dum talem ostendimus Christum, in quo dignoscitur Deus, qualis promittitur a Creatore. Obducti dehinc de Deo carnis auctore, et de Christo carnis redemptore, jam et de resurrectione carnis revincentur. Congruenter scilicet. Et hoc ferme modo dicimus ineundam cum haereticis disceptationem. Nam et ordo semper a principalibus deduci exposcit, ut de ipso prius constet, a quo dicatur dispositum esse, quod quaeritur. Atque adeo et haeretici, ex conscientia infirmitatis, nunquam ordinarie tractant. Certi enim, quam laborent in alterius divinitatis insinuatione adversus Deum mundi omnibus naturaliter notum de testimoniis operum; certe et in sacramentis priorem, et in praedicationibus manifestiorem; sub obtentu quasi urgentioris caussae, id est, ipsius humanae salutis ante omnia requirendae, a quaestionibus resurrectionis incipiunt: quia durius creditur resurrectio carnis, quam una divinitas: atque ita tractatum, viribus ordinis sui destitutum, et scrupulis potius oneratum depretiantibus carnem, paulatim alterius divinitatis temperant sensum, ex ipsa spei concussione et demutatione. Dejectus enim unusquisque vel motus de gradu ejus spei quam susceperat apud Creatorem, facile jam declinatur ad alterius spei auctorem etiam ultro suspicandum. Per diversitatem enim promissionum, diversitas insinuatur deorum. Sic multos inretitos videmus, dum ante de resurrectione carnis eliduntur, quam de unione divinitatis elidunt. Igitur, quantum ad haereticos, demonstravimus quo cuneo occurrendum sit a nobis; et occursum est jam suo quoque titulo, de Deo quidem unico, et Christo ejus, adversus Marcionem; de carne vero Domini, etiam adversus quatuor haereses; ad hanc maxime quaestionem praestruendam, uti nunc de sola carnis resurrectione ita digeram, tanquam penes nos incertum, dum sit quoque certum penes Creatorem. Nam et multi rudes, et plerique sua fide dubii et simplices; plures, quos instrui, dirigi, muniri oportebit; quia et hoc latere unio divinitatis defendetur. Sicuti enim negata carnis resurrectione, concutitur; ita vindicata, constabilitur. Animae autem salutem credo retractu carere. Omnes enim fere haeretici eam quoquo modo velint, tamen non negant. Viderit unus aliqui Lucanus, nec huic quidem substantiae parcens, quam secundum Aristotelem dissolvens, aliud quid pro ea subjicit, quasi sit tertium quiddam resurrecturum, neque anima, neque caro, id est non homo, sed ursus forsitan, qua Lucanus. Habet et iste a nobis plenissimum de omni statu animae stylum, quam imprimis immortalem tuentes, solius carnis et defectionem agnoscimus, et refectionem cum maxime asserimus; redactis in ordinarium materiae corpus, si qua et alibi pro caussarum incursione praestricta distulimus. Nam ut quaedam praelibari solemne est, ita differri necesse est, dummodo et praelibata suppleantur suo corpore, et dilata reddantur suo nomine.
pass_a_gloss: But if indeed there is some sect with God, more akin to Epicureans than to prophets, we will know what the Sadducees hear from Christ. For Christ was preserving all things hidden to uncover, directing doubts, supplementing things foretold, representing things preached; certainly the resurrection of the dead, not only through himself, but also in himself to prove. Now, however, we are prepared for other Sadducees, partisans of their opinion. Thus they acknowledge half a resurrection, namely of the soul alone; having despised the flesh, just as they also despise the Lord of the flesh. Finally, they envy no other salvation of the bodily substance, except that of another divinity, heretics. And therefore they are also forced to dispose of Christ differently, lest he be considered the creator of the flesh, and they have erred about his flesh first; or, contending for no truth, they follow Marcion and Basilides; or his own quality, according to the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles. And so it follows that they exclude the salvation of the substance of which they deny Christ to be a part; certain that it is instructed with the greatest prejudice of the resurrection, if the flesh has already risen in Christ. Therefore, we have also sent forth a volume, On the Flesh of Christ, in which we prove it solid, against the vanity of a phantom, and human, against the property of quality; whose condition has inscribed Christ as both man and son of man. For proving him to be fleshy and bodily, we also cover by prescribing that no other God is to be believed except the Creator, while we show such a Christ, in whom God is recognized, as he is promised by the Creator. Covered, then, concerning the God who is the author of the flesh, and concerning Christ, the redeemer of the flesh, they will also be convinced about the resurrection of the flesh. Fittingly, indeed. And we say that the discussion with heretics must be begun in almost this way. For the order always demands to be deduced from the principal things, so that it may be established first from whom it is said to be disposed, what is being sought. And so, even heretics, from the consciousness of weakness, never treat things in an orderly way. For they labor in the insinuation of another divinity against God, known to all the world by the testimonies of his works; certainly, also in the sacraments, prior, and in the preachings, more manifest; under the pretext of a more urgent cause, that is, the salvation of man to be sought above all, they begin from the questions of resurrection: because the resurrection of the flesh is more difficult to believe than one divinity: and thus, having treated it, destitute of the strength of their order, and burdened with scruples, rather than appreciating the flesh, they gradually temper the sense of another divinity, from the very concussion and change of hope. For each one, having been cast down or moved from the degree of hope which he had received with the Creator, easily inclines to the author of another hope, even to suspect him further. For through the diversity of promises, a diversity of gods is insinuated. So we see many entangled, while they are eliminated from the resurrection of the flesh before they are eliminated from the union of divinity. Therefore, as much as concerns heretics, we have demonstrated with what wedge we must meet them; and it has been met already in its own title, concerning the one God, and Christ his, against Marcion; concerning the flesh of the Lord, also against four heresies; to prepare for this greatest question, so that now I treat the resurrection of the flesh alone, as if it were uncertain with us, while it is also certain with the Creator. For many are unskilled, and most are doubtful and simple in their faith; many, whom it will be necessary to instruct, direct, and fortify; because even this will defend the union of divinity. For just as the negation of the resurrection of the flesh shakes it, so the vindication of it establishes it. But I believe the salvation of the soul is not to be retracted. For almost all heretics, in whatever way they wish, do not deny it. Let one Lucanus see to it, nor does he spare this substance, dissolving it according to Aristotle, and substituting another thing for it, as if there were some third thing to rise, neither soul nor flesh, that is, not man, but perhaps a bear, as Lucanus. This one also has from us a most complete style concerning the entire state of the soul, which we especially guard as immortal, recognizing both the defect and the refection of the flesh alone, and asserting it most of all; having reduced the material to an orderly body, if we have postponed anything elsewhere for the incursion of causes. For just as it is customary to prelibate certain things, so it is necessary to differ, provided that the prelibated things are supplemented with their own body, and the delayed things are rendered with their own name.

pass_b_english: If some sect actually exists with God, it owes more to Epicurus than to the prophets, and then we will learn what the Sadducees hear from Christ. Christ came to uncover everything hidden from the beginning, to direct doubts, to complete what was foretold, and to embody what was preached; above all, to prove the resurrection of the dead not only through himself but in himself. Now we face new Sadducees, partisans of that same opinion. They admit only half a resurrection—the soul's alone—because they despise the flesh, just as they despise the Lord of the flesh. No other heretics begrudge the bodily substance its salvation except those who follow a rival divinity. That forces them to recast Christ so he will not be recognized as the Creator of flesh; they go wrong about his flesh first. Some deny it any reality at all, following Marcion and Basilides; others assign it a unique quality of its own, following the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles. Consequently they exclude the salvation of the very substance of which they deny Christ is a part—certain that this substance carries the decisive warrant of the resurrection, since the flesh has already risen in Christ. That is why we published On the Flesh of Christ, proving his body solid against the phantom theory and human against the special-quality theory; the very nature of that flesh identifies him as both Man and Son of Man. By proving him fleshy and bodily, we also bar the way to any God but the Creator, because we display a Christ in whom God is recognized exactly as the Creator promised. Once the God who authored the flesh and Christ who redeemed it are established, the resurrection of the flesh follows necessarily. Fittingly so. And this is essentially how we say a debate with heretics must be opened. Proper order always demands that we start from first principles, settling first from whom a thing is said to come before we ask what it is. Heretics, conscious of their weakness, never proceed in good order. They strain to smuggle in a rival divinity against the God known to all the world by the testimony of his works—equally prior in the sacraments and more manifest in the preaching. Under the pretext of a more urgent cause, namely human salvation above all, they begin with the resurrection because the flesh's resurrection is harder to believe than one God. Once they have treated it, stripped of the strength of proper order and loaded with scruples, they depreciate the flesh rather than honor it, and so gradually adjust the sense of that rival divinity through the very shaking and alteration of hope. For each person, cast down or displaced from the degree of hope he received from the Creator, easily inclines toward the author of another hope, even to the point of adopting him. Through a diversity of promises, a diversity of gods is insinuated. We see many entangled this way: they are tripped up on the resurrection of the flesh before they are tripped up on the unity of divinity. Therefore, as far as heretics go, we have shown the wedge we must use to meet them; and the meeting has already taken place on its own ground—concerning the one God and his Christ against Marcion, and concerning the flesh of the Lord against four heresies—in preparation for this greatest question. So now I treat the resurrection of the flesh alone, as if it were uncertain with us, while it stands certain with the Creator. Many are unskilled; most are doubtful and simple in their faith; many more need to be instructed, directed, and fortified, because this very point defends the unity of divinity. Just as denying the flesh's resurrection shakes that unity, so vindicating it establishes it. I believe the salvation of the soul calls for no retraction. Nearly all heretics, whatever their system, do not deny it. Let one Lucanus attend to it—though he does not spare this substance either, dissolving it according to Aristotle and substituting something else as if a third thing were to rise, neither soul nor flesh, that is, not a human being but perhaps a bear, by Lucanus. He, too, has from us a full treatment of the entire state of the soul, which we especially guard as immortal; we acknowledge only the flesh's failing and most strongly assert its restoration. We have brought the material into orderly form, postponing anything elsewhere only when the collision of causes required it. For just as it is customary to give a foretaste of certain things, so it is necessary to delay, provided the foretasted things are completed with their proper body and the delayed things are delivered under their proper name.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the relationship between the Creator, Christ, and the resurrection of the flesh. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Latin, while Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that maintains the original's agency and doctrinal distinctions. All specific references to Marcion, Basilides, Valentinus, Apelles, and Lucanus are correctly handled. The translation of 'prelibata' as 'foretold/foretaste' and 'prelibrate' as 'prelibate/foretaste' is consistent with the context of theological anticipation.
